query: For high-entropy alloys in demanding engineering applications, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment that could falsify it?

generation.hypothesis: The addition of Zr to a high-entropy alloy can improve its resistance to thermally induced toughness loss by enhancing solid solution strengthening and grain refinement.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy with a single phase (fcc) structure
generation.intervention: Addition of Zr to the alloy
generation.conditions: Thermomechanical treatment parameters, such as hot rolling and annealing, are optimized to refine grain size and enhance solid solution strengthening
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size and solid solution strengthening
generation.mechanism: The addition of Zr leads to an increase in grain size, which can be refined through hot rolling, resulting in improved ductility and resistance to thermally induced toughness loss
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss and enhanced mechanical properties, such as yield strength and ductility
generation.boundary: The optimal amount of Zr addition and thermomechanical treatment parameters need to be determined to achieve the best results
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of how Zr addition affects the microstructure and mechanical properties of the alloy is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys with and without Zr addition, subjected to different thermomechanical treatment parameters
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Zr does not lead to improved resistance to thermally induced toughness loss and enhanced mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified

Exceptional damage-tolerance of a medium-entropy alloy CrCoNi at cryogenic temperatures

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are an intriguing new class of metallic materials that derive their properties from being multi-element systems that can crystallize as a single phase, despite containing high concentrations of five or more elements with different crystal structures. Here we examine an equiatomic medium-entropy alloy containing only three elements, CrCoNi, as a single-phase face-centred cubic solid solution, which displays strength-toughness properties that exceed those of all high-entropy alloys and most multi-phase alloys. At room temperature, the alloy shows tensile strengths of almost 1 GPa, failure strains of ∼70% and KJIc fracture-toughness values above 200 MPa m1/2; at cryogenic temperatures strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2. Such properties appear to result from continuous steady strain hardening, which acts to suppress plastic instability, resulting from pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. A strong and ductile medium-entropy alloy resists hydrogen embrittlement and corrosion

Abstract: AbstractStrong and ductile materials that have high resistance to corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement are rare and yet essential for realizing safety-critical energy infrastructures, hydrogen-based industries, and transportation solutions. Here we report how we reconcile these constraints in the form of a strong and ductile CoNiV medium-entropy alloy with face-centered cubic structure. It shows high resistance to hydrogen embrittlement at ambient temperature at a strain rate of 10−4 s−1, due to its low hydrogen diffusivity and the deformation twinning that impedes crack propagation. Moreover, a dense oxide film formed on the alloy’s surface reduces the hydrogen uptake rate, and provides high corrosion resistance in dilute sulfuric acid with a corrosion current density below 7 μA cm−2. Remarkable Enhanced Mechanical Properties of TiAlCrNbV Medium-Entropy Alloy with Zr Additions

Abstract: Most medium entropy alloys (MEAs) exhibit excellent mechanical properties, but their applications are limited because of their high density. This study explores a series of lightweight nonequiatomic Ti65(AlCrNbV)35-xZrx (x = 3, 5, 7, and 10) MEAs with a low density, high strength, and high ductility. To achieve solid solution strengthening, Zr with a large atomic radius was used. In addition, various thermomechanical treatment parameters were adopted to further improve the MEAs’ mechanical properties. The density of the MEAs was revealed to be approximately 5 g/cm3, indicating that they were lightweight. Through an X-ray diffraction analysis, the MEAs were revealed to have a single body-centered cubic structure not only in the as-cast state but also after thermomechanical treatment. In terms of mechanical properties, all the as-cast MEAs with Zr additions achieved excellent performance (>1000 MPa tensile yield strength and 20% tensile ductility).
